tagline.text: Rolling grass hills and stone-house villages on an island of wind

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–6,000 per person per day (excluding airfare)

children.text: The Philippines' northernmost province, Batanes is a cluster of remote islands closer to Taiwan than to the rest of the country, where rolling grass hills sweep endlessly toward the sea and Ivatan stone houses built to withstand typhoons complete the scene. It's hard to reach and expensive, but many consider it the most exotic and peaceful destination in the Philippines.
Batanes is the Philippines' northernmost province, made up of 10 islands scattered across the Bashi Channel, about
160 km
from the northern coast of mainland Luzon and about
190 km

from the southern tip of Taiwan. Only three islands are inhabited: Batan, home to the capital Basco; Sabtang, where traditional villages remain well preserved; and Itbayat, the largest island. With a population of roughly 18,000, it is one of the smallest provinces in the Philippines.

Batanes is often called "the Philippines that doesn't feel like the Philippines." Instead of palm-lined beaches, it has green pastures rolling gently down toward the sea, black rocky coasts where waves crash, and hills where cattle graze — scenery that brings Scotland or New Zealand to mind. Since typhoons pass through several times a year, the native Ivatan people have long built stone houses with walls nearly
1 m
thick, made of limestone and coral stone and topped with thick cogon-grass roofs. In the village of Chavayan on Sabtang Island, rows of these traditional stone houses still line the lanes today.

The people here are also famous for their honesty. The unstaffed "Honesty Coffee Shop" in Ivana, where customers calculate their own bill and leave the money themselves, has become a symbol of Batanes, and the crime rate is so low that the streets feel safe even at night.

With essentially only one flight route, airfare is expensive, and both planes and boats are frequently canceled depending on the weather, making this a demanding destination. For that reason, Batanes isn't a quick stopover but more of a slow-travel destination, best enjoyed over at least
3 nights and 4 days
, touring the islands leisurely by bicycle or tricycle. For travelers drawn to scenic photography, quiet rest, and traditional culture, it's a place worth visiting at least once in a lifetime.

blocks.title: Vayang Rolling Hills and Naidi Hill lighthouse

children.text: The Vayang Rolling Hills north of Basco are Batanes's signature scenery, with grassland rippling like waves down toward the sea. The white lighthouse on Naidi Hill, close to downtown Basco, is a favorite spot for sunset views.

A vast communal pasture in Mahatao, nicknamed "Marlboro Country" for its resemblance to the ranch in the old cigarette ads. Grazing cattle, Mount Iraya in the distance, and the Pacific cliffs all fit into one frame here.
From Radiwan Port in Ivana, a traditional boat called a faluwa takes about
30–45 minutes
to cross over to the Ivatan stone-house villages of Savidug and Chavayan. In Chavayan, you can try on the vakul, the traditional headgear worn by local women, for photos.

At Morong Beach on Sabtang Island stands a massive natural rock arch rising from the sea. It's often used as a lunch spot on Sabtang tours, and eating an Ivatan-style packed lunch on the beach here is a special experience.
On the coast east of Basco, round boulders spewed out by Mount Iraya cover the beach instead of sand. The sound of waves rolling the boulders is striking, and it's a favorite spot for sunrise.

blocks.title: Honesty Coffee Shop and House of Dakay in Ivana

children.text: At the unstaffed Honesty Coffee Shop, buy coffee and snacks and record your own purchase in the ledger to pay. Nearby, the House of Dakay is a stone house built in

earthquake.
The Saint Carlos Borromeo Church in Mahatao, the Saint Joseph Church in Ivana, and the hilltop Tukon Church (Mount Carmel Chapel), all built in the
, together showcase Batanes's distinctive stone architecture and scenery.

Renting a bicycle in Basco and riding along the coastal roads is the most authentically Batanes way to see the island. Traffic is light and the roads are well paved, but the hills are steep enough that an electric bike is worth considering.

This is effectively the only realistic means. The PAL Express Manila–Basco route ended in
October 2025
, so now the Clark–Basco (BSO) route operates daily, with a flight time of about
1 hour 15 minutes
. One-way fares vary widely, from about
during sales to over
in peak season, so booking several months ahead is essential. Check the latest flight information.
From Manila, take the P2P bus to Clark International Airport (about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
, about
one way) from NAIA Terminal 3, PITX, Cubao, and elsewhere. Flights to Basco depart at around
10 AM
, so to avoid Manila's morning traffic jams it is safer to stay in Clark or Angeles the night before.

From northern Luzon you can also use small airlines. Sky Pasada flies from Laoag, Tuguegarao, and Binalonan (Pangasinan), and Fliteline Airways flies from Tuguegarao to Basco. They are small aircraft with few seats, so they sell out early and baggage weight limits are strict, so check the conditions when booking. It is convenient for combining a northern Ilocos (Pagudpud, Laoag) trip with Batanes in one go.

There is essentially no regular passenger ferry from mainland Luzon to Batanes, only irregular cargo ships, which are not recommended for travelers. Inter-island travel uses the traditional faluwa boat. Radiwan Port on Batan Island to Sabtang Island takes about
30–45 minutes
, and Basco to Itbayat about
3–4 hours
, with cancellations on rough-sea days. Small planes also fly to Itbayat from Basco at times.
Basco Airport is right next to town, about
5–10 minutes
to your accommodation by tricycle. For island touring, choose between a tricycle tour with a driver-guide (northern or southern routes, about
per tricycle), a van tour, or renting a bicycle, e-bike, or scooter. On Sabtang Island too, tricycle tours from the port cost about
per tricycle.
The best time is from
March
to
June
. Winds and waves calm down during this period, so flights and the Sabtang faluwa run relatively reliably, the grass is green, and the sky is clear. April–
May
especially is peak season for Batanes travel, so flights and lodging fill up fast.
From
July
to
October

is typhoon season. Batanes is one of the places typhoons pass through most often in the Philippines, and when one hits, flights can be grounded for days, stranding travelers on the island. If traveling during this period, build 2–3 spare days into your itinerary.
From
November
to
February

, the strong northeast monsoon brings temperatures down to around 15–20°C, and rough seas frequently cancel boats to Sabtang and Itbayat. You can experience unusually cool weather for the Philippines, but rain and strong winds limit outdoor sightseeing considerably. Holy Week and the April–
May
school break bring the most domestic travelers, so during those periods it's safest to book flights and lodging at least three months ahead.

Most lodging is clustered in the capital, Basco, with family-run guesthouses priced around

per night. For something more special, Fundacion Pacita — a boutique lodge converted from the old studio of Filipino painter Pacita Abad — is well known; it sits on a hilltop overlooking the sea with a wonderful view, though rates are higher and rooms fill up early. With few rooms available on the island, secure your lodging along with your flight, especially in peak season.

Ivatan food is simple but distinctive. Signature dishes include uvod (banana pith minced and stir-fried with meat), lunis (pork salted and slow-cooked in oil), dibang (dried flying fish), and various seaweed and seafood dishes. Fresh lobster and fish are also available at reasonable prices. There are few large restaurants on the island, so meals are typically at your lodging or a small home-style eatery, and lunch during tours often comes as an Ivatan packed lunch wrapped in banana leaf. The coconut crab is an endangered species and protected, so even if it appears on a menu, it's best not to order it.
Starting in
June 2026
, all visitors must pre-register and pay a fee through the Batanes provincial government's online portal. Be sure to check the latest notices before you go.
The island has a few ATMs, but they often break down or run out of cash. Bring most of your cash for the trip from Manila.
Build in a spare 1–2 days between your return flight and any connecting international flight, in case of flight cancellations.
The faluwa to Sabtang is meant to depart in the calm early morning and return by around noon. Confirm with your lodging or guide the night before whether it's sailing.
The wind is strong and the weather changes fast. Bring a light windbreaker, long sleeves, and a small umbrella; from November to
February
a light coat is also needed.
Phone signal is generally good in downtown Basco but weak on the sea cliffs and in parts of Sabtang.
Restaurants close early and menus are limited, so it's convenient to arrange dinner with your lodging in advance.
The best light for photos is within
2 hours
of sunrise and the
2 hours
before sunset. Midday sun is harsh and there's little shade.
During typhoon season (July–
October
), you could be stranded on the island for days. Get travel insurance and set aside an emergency budget.
Most cliffside viewpoints have no railing. Don't get close to the edge on windy days.
The cattle and goats on the grassland belong to local residents. Don't cross pasture fences, and don't startle the animals.
The stone houses are still lived in by residents. Always ask permission before looking inside or taking photos.
Unstaffed honor-system shops like the Honesty Coffee Shop are part of Batanes's culture of trust. Make sure not to skip paying.
The biggest variable in a Batanes trip is the weather. Plan generously, assuming flights and boats can be canceled at any time.
